en: Let me think; I would choose the blue one.
tamil: கொஞ்சம் யோசிக்கிறேன்; நான் நீல நிறத்தை தான் எடுப்பேன்.
context: Choosing a colour in a shop.
explain: 'Would choose' gives a polite choice. It sounds softer than 'I choose'.
usage: Say it in a shop or at home when someone asks you to pick one thing.
leelaQ: Which colour would you choose for a new bag?
answer: I would choose a black bag because it goes with everything.

en: Do you think it is too late to start now?
tamil: இப்போ ஆரம்பிக்கிறது ரொம்ப லேட்னு நினைக்கிறீங்களா?
context: Asking if there is still time.
explain: 'Too late' means there is no more time. 'Do you think' asks for an opinion.
usage: Use it when you plan a task or a journey and time is short.
leelaQ: Is it ever too late to learn something new?
answer: No, I think we can learn new things at any age.

en: She is going to say yes because the offer is good.
tamil: ஆபர் நல்லா இருக்கறதால அவ ஆமான்னு தான் சொல்லுவா.
context: Predicting a friend's answer.
explain: 'Going to' is used to predict something you feel sure about.
usage: Use it when you guess what someone will decide, based on what you know.
leelaQ: What do you think your friend is going to do this weekend?
answer: I think my friend is going to visit his village this weekend.

en: Please give me a reason for your choice.
tamil: உங்க தேர்வுக்கு ஒரு காரணம் சொல்லுங்க.
context: Asking someone to justify a choice.
explain: 'Give me a reason' asks for an explanation in a polite, short way.
usage: Use it in a class, a meeting or at home when a choice seems strange.
leelaQ: What reason do you give when you choose something?
answer: I say the reason clearly, like it is cheaper or more comfortable.

en: I am thinking that we should change the plan.
tamil: நாம திட்டத்தை மாத்தணும்னு நான் யோசிச்சுட்டு இருக்கேன்.
context: Gently suggesting a change of plan.
explain: 'I am thinking that...' opens a suggestion slowly and politely.
usage: Use it with a team or family when you want to suggest something new without sounding pushy.
leelaQ: Have you ever changed a plan at the last minute?
answer: Yes, I changed my trip plan at the last minute because of rain.

en: For me, mornings are the best time to study.
tamil: என்னைப் பொறுத்தவரை படிக்க காலை நேரம் தான் ரொம்ப நல்லது.
context: Telling your best study time.
explain: 'For me' shows this is your own view, not a rule for everyone.
usage: Use it when friends talk about study or work habits.
leelaQ: What is the best time for you to study or work?
answer: For me, early morning is the best time because the house is quiet.

en: How do you feel about working on Saturdays?
tamil: சனிக்கிழமையும் வேலை செய்றதை பத்தி உங்களுக்கு எப்படி இருக்கு?
context: Asking about a work change.
explain: 'How do you feel about...?' asks for a feeling or opinion about a topic.
usage: Use it when a manager or a colleague talks about a new schedule.
leelaQ: How do you feel about waking up early?
answer: I feel fine about it because I love the quiet morning time.

en: I have seen both films, and the second one is better.
tamil: நான் ரெண்டு படமும் பார்த்துட்டேன், ரெண்டாவது தான் நல்லா இருக்கு.
context: Comparing two films you watched.
explain: 'Have seen' means you did it before now. 'Better' is the comparative of 'good'.
usage: Use it when friends ask you which movie to watch.
leelaQ: Which film have you seen recently, and was it good?
answer: I have seen a Tamil film recently, and it was really good.

en: I don't think the film was worth the money.
tamil: அந்த படம் கொடுத்த காசுக்கு தகுதியானதுன்னு நான் நினைக்கல.
context: Giving a negative opinion on a film.
explain: In English we say 'I don't think it is...' instead of 'I think it is not...'.
usage: Use it when friends ask if a film or a product was good.
leelaQ: What was the last thing you felt was not worth the money?
answer: A very costly coffee was not worth the money for me.

en: It depends on the budget, but I would go by train.
tamil: அது பட்ஜெட்டை பொறுத்தது, ஆனா நான் ட்ரெயின்ல தான் போவேன்.
context: Giving a conditional opinion.
explain: 'It depends on' means the answer changes with the situation.
usage: Use it when someone asks for advice and the best choice is not clear.
leelaQ: What does your travel choice depend on?
answer: My travel choice depends on the time and the ticket price.

en: Would you like to go by metro or by auto?
tamil: நீங்க மெட்ரோலயா, இல்ல ஆட்டோலயா போக விரும்புறீங்க?
context: Offering travel choices to a friend.
explain: 'Would you like...?' is a polite way to offer a choice.
usage: Ask it when you plan a trip with a friend or a guest.
leelaQ: What do you like to take for short trips in your city?
answer: I like to take an auto because it is quick and easy.

en: My father believes that saving early is very important.
tamil: சீக்கிரமே சேமிக்கிறது ரொம்ப முக்கியம்னு என் அப்பா நம்புறாரு.
context: Sharing your father's view on saving.
explain: 'Believes that...' reports another person's opinion.
usage: Use it when you talk about what elders at home advise.
leelaQ: What advice about money do your parents give?
answer: My parents say I should save some money every month.

en: Can you suggest a good restaurant for dinner?
tamil: டின்னருக்கு ஒரு நல்ல ஹோட்டல் சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a local for a recommendation.
explain: 'Can you suggest...?' is a simple request for a recommendation.
usage: Ask a colleague or a hotel receptionist when you are new to a city.
leelaQ: Can you suggest a good place to eat in your town?
answer: Yes, I can suggest a small hotel near the bus stand for tasty meals.

en: That idea sounds interesting, let us try it.
tamil: அந்த ஐடியா சுவாரஸ்யமா இருக்கு, முயற்சி பண்ணலாம்.
context: Accepting a new suggestion.
explain: 'Sounds + adjective' tells your reaction to what you hear.
usage: Use it at work or with friends when you like someone's suggestion.
leelaQ: What new idea would you like to try this year?
answer: I would like to try learning the guitar this year.

en: The old phone was slow, so I bought a new one.
tamil: பழைய போன் மெதுவா இருந்துச்சு, அதனால புதுசு வாங்கினேன்.
context: Giving a reason for buying a phone.
explain: 'So' shows a result: the phone was slow, so I bought a new one.
usage: Use it when someone asks why you changed something.
leelaQ: Why did you buy your current phone?
answer: I bought it because my old phone was slow and the camera was bad.

en: I agree with most of what you said.
tamil: நீங்க சொன்னதுல பெரும்பாலானதை நான் ஒத்துக்கிறேன்.
context: Agreeing partly with a speaker.
explain: 'Most of' means almost all. It lets you agree without agreeing to everything.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you accept the main idea but have small doubts.
leelaQ: What was the last thing you agreed with someone about?
answer: I agreed with my brother that we should visit our grandmother.

en: In my view, small shops give better service.
tamil: என் பார்வையில சின்ன கடைகள் தான் நல்ல சேவை தராங்க.
context: Giving a view about shops.
explain: 'In my view' is another way to say 'in my opinion'. 'Better' compares with big shops.
usage: Use it when friends discuss shopping in a mall or in a local shop.
leelaQ: Do you prefer small shops or big malls?
answer: I prefer small shops because the owner knows me well.

en: What is your opinion on online shopping?
tamil: ஆன்லைன் ஷாப்பிங் பத்தி உங்க கருத்து என்ன?
context: Asking for someone's view.
explain: 'Your opinion on...' is a polite and formal way to ask what someone thinks.
usage: Use it in a discussion, an interview or a class.
leelaQ: How often do you shop online?
answer: I shop online two or three times a month for small things.

en: Let us compare both offers before we decide.
tamil: முடிவு பண்றதுக்கு முன்னாடி ரெண்டு ஆபரையும் ஒப்பிட்டு பார்ப்போம்.
context: Suggesting a careful comparison.
explain: 'Let us' makes a suggestion that includes both speaker and listener.
usage: Use it with family or colleagues when you must choose between two deals.
leelaQ: How do you compare two offers before you buy?
answer: I check the price, the quality and the reviews of both offers.

en: We are discussing which restaurant is best for dinner.
tamil: இன்னைக்கு டின்னருக்கு எந்த ஹோட்டல் நல்லதுன்னு நாங்க பேசிட்டு இருக்கோம்.
context: Telling someone what you are talking about.
explain: 'Are discussing' shows the talk is happening right now.
usage: Say it on the phone when someone asks what you and your friends are doing.
leelaQ: What are you and your friends discussing these days?
answer: We are discussing a trip to Ooty for the long weekend.

en: I am sure you will like this place.
tamil: இந்த இடம் உங்களுக்கு கண்டிப்பா பிடிக்கும்னு நான் உறுதியா சொல்றேன்.
context: Recommending a place to a friend.
explain: 'I am sure' shows strong belief. 'Will like' talks about the future.
usage: Use it when you take a friend to a favourite cafe or tourist spot.
leelaQ: Which place would you take a new friend to?
answer: I would take my friend to the beach because it is calm in the evening.

en: Are you going to choose the cheaper phone?
tamil: நீங்க விலை குறைவான போனை தான் எடுக்கப் போறீங்களா?
context: Asking about a buying decision.
explain: 'Are you going to...?' asks about a plan or a decision.
usage: Ask it when a friend is choosing between two phones.
leelaQ: What do you look at first when you buy a phone?
answer: I look at the battery and the camera before the price.

en: Rice is my favourite because it fills me up.
tamil: சாதம் தான் என் பிடிச்சது, ஏன்னா வயிறு நிறையும்.
context: Giving a reason for liking a food.
explain: 'Because' gives the reason for a feeling or choice.
usage: Use it when someone asks why you love a certain food.
leelaQ: What is your favourite food, and why?
answer: My favourite food is dosa because it is tasty and light.

en: That is not what I meant.
tamil: நான் சொன்னது அந்த அர்த்தத்துல இல்ல.
context: Correcting a misunderstanding.
explain: 'Not what I meant' clears a misunderstanding without blaming the other person.
usage: Use it when someone takes your words the wrong way.
leelaQ: How do you clear a misunderstanding with a friend?
answer: I explain again slowly and say sorry if my words were confusing.

en: I think the exam was easier than last time.
tamil: போன தடவையை விட இந்த தடவை பரீட்சை ஈசியா இருந்துச்சுன்னு நினைக்கிறேன்.
context: Talking about an exam with a classmate.
explain: 'Easier than' compares two things. 'Last time' means the previous exam.
usage: Use it with classmates right after coming out of an exam hall.
leelaQ: How did your last exam or interview go?
answer: My last interview went well, and the questions were easy.
